stem: Configure firewall rules to meet the scenario. Rules are evaluated top-down; first match wins.
scenario: Allow DNS (UDP 53) from internal subnet 10.50.0.0/16 to the DNS resolver 10.50.1.10. Allow NTP (UDP 123) from 10.50.0.0/16 to 10.50.1.20. Deny all other UDP from 10.50.0.0/16 to those two hosts.
explanation: Permit only DNS to the resolver and NTP to the time server from the internal range, then explicitly deny other UDP to those hosts so first-match evaluation enforces least privilege.

stem: Select ALL hosts that show signs of compromise or malicious activity based on the logs.
scenario: Overnight SIEM alerts flagged unusual authentication and process activity. Review the excerpts and select hosts that require investigation.

logs.message: Successful interactive login for adev from 10.1.4.22 (expected VPN)
mimikatz.exe executed by local admin; LSASS memory access flagged
New scheduled task \Updater created running C:\Users\Public\svc.bat
Screen lock engaged after idle timeout (policy)
Outbound SSH to 203.0.113.88:22 from www-data; first-seen destination
Print job completed for user jlee

explanation: SRV-FILE02 shows credential dumping and persistence via a suspicious scheduled task. SRV-WEB01 shows unexpected outbound SSH from the web service account to a newly seen host. The workstation login and printer events look benign.

stem: Order the forensic evidence handling steps correctly from first to last.
scenario: A laptop suspected of compromise must be preserved for investigation. Arrange the steps in the proper order.

steps.text: Isolate the system and document the scene / chain-of-custody start
Capture volatile memory if powered on and justified
Create a forensic disk image and verify hashes
Analyze working copies and report findings

explanation: Preserve and document first, capture volatile data while available, image and hash for integrity, then analyze copies—not the original evidence.

stem: Place the BEST security control in each Zero Trust access path slot.
scenario: Remote user → [Broker] → App → [Data]. Choose appropriate controls for a Zero Trust design.

slots.label: Access broker / edge
options: ZTNA / identity-aware proxy with device posture checks
slots.answer: ZTNA / identity-aware proxy with device posture checks

slots.label: Application tier
options: Mutual TLS and least-privilege service accounts
Hard-coded SQL sa password in the UI
slots.answer: Mutual TLS and least-privilege service accounts

slots.label: Data store
options: Encryption at rest + column-level access controls
Public read ACL for all objects
slots.answer: Encryption at rest + column-level access controls

explanation: Zero Trust uses an identity/posture-aware broker, strong app authentication, and tightly controlled encrypted data stores—not open remote protocols or public data ACLs.

stem: Match each attack technique to the BEST description.
scenario: Associate the attack name with what it primarily does.

pairs.right: Few common passwords tried across many accounts
Reuse of leaked username/password pairs on other sites
Authenticate using captured NTLM hashes without cracking
Fraudulent payment or gift-card requests via email impersonation

distractors: Flooding a target with ICMP only
Physical theft of a badge printer
explanation: Spraying avoids lockouts with common passwords; stuffing replays breach dumps; PtH reuses hashes; BEC social-engineers finance workflows.

stem: Configure firewall rules for a three-tier app. Rules are evaluated top-down; first match wins.
scenario: Allow TCP 443 from any Internet client to DMZ load balancer 172.16.10.5. Allow TCP 8080 only from 172.16.10.5 to app server 10.20.20.10. Allow TCP 5432 only from 10.20.20.10 to DB 10.20.30.10. Deny all other traffic to 10.20.20.10 and 10.20.30.10.
explanation: Internet reaches only the LB on 443; the LB alone talks to the app on 8080; only the app reaches the DB on 5432; explicit denies protect the internal tiers from other sources.
